# 1. Introduction

Inte previous notebook we gave an introduction to Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), the maximum likelihood estimation vía the forward algorithm and the EM algorithm version for the estimation of HMM. We focused on the fudamentals and we use primary tools in the code snippetsinstead of specificly designed libraries for the estimation of HMM using the fquentist approach.

In this notebook, our focus is to expand the theory of HMM by introduciong the Bayesian approach which treats the parameters of the Markov process and the state-dependent distributions as random variables. As we will illustrate later, an advantadge of the Bayesian approach over the frequentist approach is that maximum likelihood estimations can get stuck on a single point when it is possible that posterior distributions (that is the distribution of the parameters) present multiple local maxima. 

Here we expand the theory by introducing a Bayesian approach to HMM, the label switching problem and genuine multimodality.


# 2. Bayesian HMM

The Bayesian approach relies on Bayes' theorem, which states that the conditional distribution of a set of random variables $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ given a set of observations $\mathbf{y}$, called the posterior distribution, is equal to the product of the prior distribution of the parameters $p(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ and the conditional distribution of the observations given the parameters $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})$, divided by the marginal distribution of $\mathbf{y}$, $p(\mathbf{y}) = \int p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\, p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})\, d\boldsymbol{\theta}$, which ensures that the posterior integrates to one [@gelman2013bda, ch. 1]:

$$
p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) = \frac{p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\, p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})}{p(\mathbf{y})}.
$${#eq-bayes}

Recall that $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})$, viewed as a function of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ for fixed observations, is the likelihood function $L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})$. Moreover, since the normalizing constant $p(\mathbf{y})$ does not depend on $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, it can be omitted, and Bayes' theorem can be written as the posterior being proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior:

$$
p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})\, p(\boldsymbol{\theta}).
$$ {#eq-posterior-unnorm}

This last expression is the core of Bayesian inference. In most models of practical interest, the integral defining $p(\mathbf{y})$ has no closed form and cannot be computed numerically in high dimensions, so the posterior is only available up to a normalizing constant. Several methods have been developed to perform Bayesian inference under this limitation, among which Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods stand out given that only require evaluating the unnormalized posterior in @eq-posterior-unnorm, since the normalizing constant cancels out when comparing the posterior density at two different values of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ [@gelman2013bda, ch. 10].

## 2.1 Parameters and prior distributions of a Bayesian HMM {#sec-priors}

Recall that an HMM is a state-space model consisting of an observation process $\{Y_t\}$ and an unobserved Markov process $\{C_t\}$ taking values in a finite set of states $\{1, \dots, m\}$ [@zucchini2016]. The realization of the observation process, $\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \dots, y_T)$, is the data on which the posterior in @eq-bayes is conditioned.

The parameters governing $\{C_t\}$ are the initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ and the transition probability matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, while each of the $m$ state-dependent distributions, also known as emission distributions, has its own parameters $\boldsymbol{\eta}_j$, $j = 1, \dots, m$. We collect all of them in the parameter vector

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\boldsymbol{\delta}, \boldsymbol{\Gamma}, \boldsymbol{\eta}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{\eta}_m),
$$

so that specifying a Bayesian HMM amounts to specifying a prior distribution $p(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ over each of these components.

Regarding the initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ if it is stationary, then it can be derived from $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ so it leaves $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. In this notebook we make the assumption that the Markov process is homogeneous and stationary.

### 2.1.1 Transition probability matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$

Each row of the transition probability matrix, $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i = (\gamma_{i1}, \dots, \gamma_{im})$ for $i = 1, \dots, m$, is a vector of non-negative entries that sum to one. In other words, it belongs to the probability *simplex*

$$
\Delta^{m-1} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m : x_j \geq 0,\ \sum_{j=1}^{m} x_j = 1 \right\},
$$

the $(m-1)$-dimensional set of all probability distributions over $m$ elements [@boyd2004convex, p. 33]. A natural choice for the prior for vectors in $\Delta^{m-1}$ is the Dirichlet distribution, whose support is precisely this set [@frigyik2010dirichlet]. We therefore assume that the rows of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ are independent and that each follows a Dirichlet distribution,

$$
\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i), \qquad \boldsymbol{\tau}_i = (\tau_{i1}, \dots, \tau_{im}), \quad \tau_{ij} > 0,
$$

with density

$$
p(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \mid \boldsymbol{\tau}_i) = \frac{1}{B(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i)} \prod_{j=1}^{m} \gamma_{ij}^{\tau_{ij} - 1},
\qquad
B(\boldsymbol{\tau}_i) = \frac{\prod_{j=1}^{m} \Gamma(\tau_{ij})}{\Gamma\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m} \tau_{ij}\right)},
$$ {#eq-dirichlet}

where $\Gamma(\cdot)$ denotes the gamma function and does not have to be confused with the transition probability matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$.

The concentration parameters $\boldsymbol{\tau}_i$ control the shape of this prior. They determine its mean, $E[\gamma_{ij}] = \tau_{ij} / \tau_{i0}$ with $\tau_{i0} = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \tau_{ij}$, and how concentrated it is around that mean: the larger $\tau_{i0}$, the more informative the prior.

Following [@leosbarajas2018] and [@gallegosherrada2026], we set $\boldsymbol{\tau}_i = \mathbf{1}_m$ for all rows. Besides its simplicity, this choice treats all states symmetrically, so the prior is invariant to a relabeling of the states; the consequences of this property are discussed in @sec-label-switching. Under this choice, @eq-dirichlet reduces to

$$
p(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \mid \boldsymbol{\tau}_i = \mathbf{1}_m) = \frac{\Gamma(m)}{\prod_{j=1}^{m} \Gamma(1)} \prod_{j=1}^{m} \gamma_{ij}^{0} = (m-1)!, \qquad \boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \in \Delta^{m-1}.
$$ {#eq-dirichlet-uniform}

Since this density does not depend on $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i$, the $\text{Dir}(\mathbf{1}_m)$ prior is uniform on the simplex, with the constant $(m-1)!$ being the reciprocal of the volume of $\Delta^{m-1}$. Uniformity on the simplex, however, does not imply uniformity on each entry: the marginal prior of each $\gamma_{ij}$ is $\text{Beta}(1, m-1)$, which places more mass near zero as $m$ grows. In particular, it favors a priori low persistence in each state, i.e., small values of $\gamma_{ii}$.

### 2.1.2 Initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$

Since the entries of the initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ must add to one and are all non-negative, it also has support on the probability simplex $\Delta^{m-1}$. 

We can treat $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ as a free parameter with its own prior distribution or to assume that the Markov process is stationary, so that $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ is its stationary distribution.

Stationarity means that the chain is already in equilibrium when the observation process starts, so the distribution of the states does not change from one time point to the next [@zucchini2016]

$$
\boldsymbol{\delta} \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = \boldsymbol{\delta}, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{m} \delta_j = 1.
$$ {#eq-stationary}

When the chain is irreducible, that is, when every state can be reached from any other state within a finite number of steps, the stationary distribution exists and is unique [@sargent2022networks, Theorem 4.1.1]. 

Under the $\text{Dir}(\mathbf{1}_m)$ prior of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, this condition holds with probability one: since the Dirichlet distribution is continuous on the simplex, no entry $\gamma_{ij}$ is exactly zero with probability one, so every state can be reached from any other in a single step. The stationary distribution is then given by

$$
\boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathbf{1}_m \left( \mathbf{I}_m - \boldsymbol{\Gamma} + \mathbf{U} \right)^{-1},
$$ {#eq-stationary-solution}

where $\mathbf{1}_m$ is a row vector of ones, $\mathbf{I}_m$ is the $m \times m$ identity matrix and $\mathbf{U}$ is the $m \times m$ matrix of ones [@zucchini2016]. Under the stationarity assumption, $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ is no longer a parameter but a deterministic function of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, so it requires no prior of its own: its prior distribution is the one induced by the prior on the rows of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$.

In this notebook we assume that the observation process starts when the chain is stationary and hence $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ is the stationary distribution. 

### 2.1.3 State-dependent distributions

Unlike the transition probabilities, the parameters of the state-dependent distributions do not share a common support, so there is no single prior that applies to every model. However, the choice can be guided by the support of each parameter. For example, real-valued parameters such as means call for priors on $\mathbb{R}$, while positive parameters such as standard deviations or rates call for priors on $(0, \infty)$.

Another criterion for choosing priors is the algorithm used to draw samples from the posterior distribution. Gibbs samplers commonly rely on conjugate priors, which yield posterior conditional distributions in closed form given the hidden states. *Stan*, which we use later in this notebook, does not require conjugacy, so priors can be chosen for what they express rather than for their algebraic convenience.

When the state-dependent distributions are normal, the conjugate choice is a normal prior on each mean $\mu_j$ and an inverse-gamma prior on each variance $\sigma_j^2$ [@gelman2013bda]. However, inverse-gamma priors with small parameters can be highly influential when a state has few observations, so weakly informative priors on the standard deviation, such as a half-normal or half-$t$ distribution, are often preferred [@gelman2006prior; @leosbarajas2018]. When the observations are counts modeled with a Poisson distribution in each state, a gamma prior on each rate $\lambda_j$ is a natural choice, both because it is conjugate and because it has the appropriate support, although in *Stan* only the latter matters. 

In this notebook we work with normal state-dependent distributions and use

$$
\mu_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, s_0^2), \qquad \sigma_j \sim \text{half-}\mathcal{N}(0, s_1^2), \qquad j = 1, \dots, m.
$$ {#eq-emission-priors}

Two features of these priors are important for what follows. First, the same prior is assigned to the parameters of every state, as was done for the rows of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, so that no state is distinguished a priori. The consequences of this choice are discussed in @sec-exchangeability. Second, the priors are weakly informative rather than vague. In mixture models and HMMs, improper or nearly flat priors on the state-dependent parameters can lead to improper posterior distributions, since there is always a configuration in which some state is assigned no observations and the data provide no information about its parameters [@fruhwirth2006].

## 2.2 Likelihood via the forward algorithm

The last element needed to assemble the unnormalized posterior distribution is the likelihood. In the previous notebook we showed that, by summing over all possible sequences of hidden states, the likelihood of an HMM can be written as the matrix product

$$
L_T = \boldsymbol{\delta}\, \mathbf{P}(y_1)\, \boldsymbol{\Gamma}\, \mathbf{P}(y_2) \cdots \boldsymbol{\Gamma}\, \mathbf{P}(y_T)\, \mathbf{1}_m^\top,
$$ {#eq-likelihood}

where $\mathbf{P}(y) = \text{diag}\big(p_1(y), \dots, p_m(y)\big)$ is the diagonal matrix of state-dependent densities evaluated at $y$ [@zucchini2016]. In the notation of this notebook, $L_T = L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})$, and under the stationarity assumption $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ is the function of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ given in @eq-stationary-solution. The forward algorithm evaluates @eq-likelihood at a cost that grows linearly in $T$, instead of the $m^T$ terms of the explicit sum over state sequences. In practice, the recursion is carried out on the log scale, since the product of $T$ densities quickly underflows to zero [@leosbarajas2018].

Assuming that the rows of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ and the parameters of each state are a priori independent, the log of the unnormalized posterior in @eq-posterior-unnorm becomes

$$
\log p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) = \log L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i \mid \mathbf{1}_m) + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \log p(\boldsymbol{\eta}_j) + \text{const.}
$$ {#eq-log-posterior}

No term for $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ appears, since under stationarity it carries no prior of its own. Each term of @eq-log-posterior corresponds to one statement in the Stan program presented below.

## 2.3 Exchangeable priors and posterior symmetry {#sec-exchangeability}

In this section we show that relabeling the hidden states leaves the posterior unchanged. This follows from the likelihood being invariant to the labels and from the priors being exchangeable, that is, treating all states in the same way [@jasra2005]. The resulting symmetry is what distinguishes the modes due to relabeling from genuinely different ones.

Consider an HMM with $m$ states and label them *state 1*, *state 2*, ..., *state m*. Note that this labeling from a mathematical perspective is irrelevant since the name *state 1* initially assigned to a specific state can be assigned to any other state and the same goes to every other state. Under this situation, you can obtain $m!$ different labelings.

Formally, each relabeling corresponds to a permutation $\nu$ of the labels $\{1, \dots, m\}$, and we denote by $S_m$ the set of all $m!$ such permutations [@jasra2005]. Applying a permutation $\nu \in S_m$ to the parameters of the HMM yields the relabeled parameter vector $\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})$, defined by

$$
\delta'_i = \delta_{\nu(i)}, \qquad \gamma'_{ij} = \gamma_{\nu(i)\nu(j)}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}'_j = \boldsymbol{\eta}_{\nu(j)}, \qquad i, j = 1, \dots, m.
$$ {#eq-permutation}

where $\nu \in S_{m}$ is the set of all $m!$ permutations of $1,2,...,m$.

For example, with $m = 2$ there are two permutations, the identity, which leaves the labels unchanged, and $\nu(1) = 2$, $\nu(2) = 1$, which swaps them. Applying the latter to @eq-permutation gives

$$
\boldsymbol{\delta}' = (\delta_2, \delta_1), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}' = \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_{22} & \gamma_{21} \\ \gamma_{12} & \gamma_{11} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
(\boldsymbol{\eta}'_1, \boldsymbol{\eta}'_2) = (\boldsymbol{\eta}_2, \boldsymbol{\eta}_1).
$$

Both parameter vectors describe exactly the same model, since the state previously called 2 is now called 1, together with its initial probability, its transition probabilities and its state-dependent parameters. Only the names have changed.

Note that relabeling the states does not change the likelihood. To see this, recall that @eq-likelihood is a compact form of the sum, over all possible $m^T$ state sequences $(c_1, \dots, c_T)$, of the terms $\delta_{c_1} p_{c_1}(y_1) \prod_{t=2}^{T} \gamma_{c_{t-1} c_t}\, p_{c_t}(y_t)$. By @eq-permutation, the term of the sequence $(c_1, \dots, c_T)$ evaluated at $\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ equals the term of the sequence $(\nu(c_1), \dots, \nu(c_T))$ evaluated at $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. Since every sequence appears exactly once in the sum, relabeling only reorders its terms, and therefore $L(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mid \mathbf{y}) = L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})$ for every $\nu \in S_m$.

To see this, consider $m=2$ states and $T=2$ observations. In this case we have 4 possible sequences, so the likelihood is

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) =\; & \delta_1\, p_1(y_1)\, \gamma_{11}\, p_1(y_2) + \delta_1\, p_1(y_1)\, \gamma_{12}\, p_2(y_2) \\
+\; & \delta_2\, p_2(y_1)\, \gamma_{21}\, p_1(y_2) + \delta_2\, p_2(y_1)\, \gamma_{22}\, p_2(y_2),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-likelihood-ex}

where the four terms correspond to the sequences $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$ and $(2,2)$. Now consider the permutation that swaps the labels, $\nu(1) = 2$ and $\nu(2) = 1$. By @eq-permutation, the term of the sequence $(1,2)$ evaluated at $\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ is

$$
\delta'_1\, p'_1(y_1)\, \gamma'_{12}\, p'_2(y_2) = \delta_2\, p_2(y_1)\, \gamma_{21}\, p_1(y_2),
$$

which is the term of the sequence $(2,1)$ in @eq-likelihood-ex. 

In the same way, the terms of $(1,1)$, $(2,1)$ and $(2,2)$ evaluated at $\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ equal the terms of $(2,2)$, $(1,2)$ and $(1,1)$ evaluated at $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. The four terms are therefore the same, only in a different order, and $L(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mid \mathbf{y}) = L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})$. Thus, the likelihood is invariant to relabeling of the states.


The prior distribution is also invariant to relabeling, because it treats all states in the same way. Consider again $m = 2$ and the permutation that swaps the labels. The rows of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ are exchanged and their entries reordered, but since the $\text{Dir}(\mathbf{1}_m)$ prior is uniform on the simplex, every row receives the same density before and after the swap. The stationary distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ is computed from $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, so its entries are swapped as well and no additional term appears. 

A prior with this property, which assigns the same density to every relabeling of the parameters, is called exchangeable [@fruhwirth2001; @jasra2005].

Finally, the state-dependent parameters $\boldsymbol{\eta}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{\eta}_2$ are exchanged, and since both states share the same prior, the product $p(\boldsymbol{\eta}_1)\, p(\boldsymbol{\eta}_2)$ does not change. The same argument holds for any $m$ and any permutation, so $p(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ for every $\nu \in S_m$. It is important to note, however, if we assign different priors to different states, for instance a prior centered at a low value for $\mu_1$ and at a high value for $\mu_2$, this invariance would no longer hold.

Since both the likelihood and the prior are invariant to relabeling, so is their product in @eq-posterior-unnorm, and the posterior distribution satisfies

$$
p(\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mid \mathbf{y}) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) \qquad \text{for every } \nu \in S_m.
$$ {#eq-posterior-symmetry}

A posterior satisfying @eq-posterior-symmetry is said to be symmetric with respect to the labels, since every point $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ has $m!$ counterparts $\nu(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with exactly the same posterior density.

Although relabeling leaves the posterior unchanged, it becomes problematic in practice when the posterior is explored with MCMC methods. By @eq-posterior-symmetry, the marginal posterior distributions of the state-dependent parameters coincide across states, so that, for instance, $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ have the same marginal posterior. A sampler that has converged to this symmetric posterior therefore moves between the $m!$ symmetric regions of high posterior density, and averages of state-specific quantities, such as the posterior mean of $\mu_1$, become meaningless [@jasra2005; @papastamoulis2016]. This phenomenon is known as *label switching* and methods for alleviating this phenomenon are discussed in @sec-label-switching.

## 2.4 Implementation in Stan {#sec-stan-implementation}

To draw samples from the posterior distribution of the HMM we use *Stan*, a popular open-source probabilistic programming language designed for specifying statistical models and performing Bayesian inference [@carpenter2017]. Models are written in *Stan*'s own language and can be run from several environments through interfaces such as *CmdStanPy* for *Python*, *CmdStanR* for *R* and *Stan.jl* for *Julia*. In this notebook we use *CmdStanPy*. Details on installation and usage are available on the official [website](https://mc-stan.org) and in the introductory tutorial by @carpenter2023.

*Stan* makes Bayesian inference by using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), an MCMC method that relies on techniques from differential geometry to generate transitions spanning the full marginal variance, eliminating the random component of other classes of MCMC algorithms such as Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs samplers [@betancourt2013hamiltonian].

To illustrate the ideas presented so far, we use univariate data simulated from a 2-state HMM with a moderately persistent transition probability matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$, whose stationary distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta} = (0.6,\ 0.4)$ is used as the initial distribution. The state-dependent distributions are normal with well-separated means, $\mu_1 = -2$ and $\mu_2 = 2$, and a common variance $\sigma^2 = 1$. We simulate $T = 500$ observations. These values are summarized in @tbl-sim-params.

The following *Python* code simulates the data from the HMM in @tbl-sim-params and stores it in the `data/` folder at the root of the repository. The file contains the observations $y_t$ together with the true hidden states $C_t$, which are not used for inference but allow us to assess the results later. We keep the simulation and the inference as separate steps, so that the model reads the data from a file exactly as it would in a real application, without access to how the data were generated. This also allows the same dataset to be reused in the following notebooks.

``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Seed for reproducibility
np.random.seed(0)

# States
m = 2
states = np.arange(m)

# Transition probability matrix
Gamma = np.array([[0.8, 0.2], [0.3, 0.7]])

# Stationary distribution
delta = np.array([0.6, 0.4])

# Observaton process parameters
mu = np.array([-2, 2])
sigma = np.array([1, 1])

# Arrays for the results
T = 500
C = np.zeros(T, dtype=int) # Vector to store the state sequence
Y = np.zeros(T) # Vector to store the simulated data

# Initial values
C[0] = np.random.choice(states, p=delta)
Y[0] = np.random.normal(loc=mu[C[0]], scale=sigma[C[0]])

for t in range(1, T):
    C[t] = np.random.choice(states, p=Gamma[C[t-1]])
    Y[t] = np.random.normal(loc=mu[C[t]], scale=sigma[C[t]])

# Plot the data
fig, ax = plt.subplots(ncols = 2, figsize=(10,5))

ax[0].plot(np.arange(T), Y, color='#77918e', linestyle="-.") # Observation process
ax[0].set_title("Simulated data from a two state HMM")


bins = np.linspace(Y.min(), Y.max(), 31)

ax[1].hist(Y[C == 0], bins=bins, alpha=0.7, color="#ac65c2", label="State 1")
ax[1].hist(Y[C == 1], bins=bins, alpha=0.7, color="#eba834", label="State 2")
ax[1].set_xlabel("$y_t$")
ax[1].set_ylabel("Frequency")
ax[1].set_xlabel("$y_t$")
ax[1].set_title("Histograms of the simulated data")
ax[1].legend(frameon=False)

for i in range(2):
    ax[i].spines["top"].set_visible(False)
    ax[i].spines["right"].set_visible(False)
    ax[i].grid(True, axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
    ax[i].set_axisbelow(True)
    

# Save the data in a tabular format for illustration process
t = np.arange(1, T + 1)
np.savetxt(
    "../data/02_hmm_2state.csv",
    np.column_stack([t, C + 1, Y]),
    delimiter=",",
    header="t,C,y",
    comments="",
    fmt=["%d", "%d", "%.6f"],
)

# Simulation checks
print("Proportion of tie in each state")
print("State 1:", float(np.sum(C))/T)
print("State 2:", 1-float(np.sum(C))/T)


# Save the data for stan in JSON
from cmdstanpy import write_stan_json

write_stan_json("../data/02_hmm_2state.json", {"T": T, "m": m, "y": Y})
```

In order to perform Bayesian inference with *Stan*, the model should be written a program stored in a file with the extension `.stan`. A *Stan* program does not describe how to sample from the posterior. Instead, it specifies the log of the unnormalized posterior density in @eq-log-posterior, and *Stan* computes its gradient automatically and explores it with the No-U-Turn Sampler, a variant of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [@carpenter2017]. The program is organized in blocks that must appear in a fixed order. In this notebook we use four of them.

- `data` declares the quantities that are passed to the program and remain fixed, such as the number of observations and the observations themselves.
- `parameters` declares the unknown quantities whose posterior distribution we want to explore. Constraints on these declarations, such as positivity , define the space in which the sampler moves.
- `transformed parameters` defines quantities computed deterministically from the parameters, which are recomputed at each iteration and stored in the output alongside the parameters.
- `model` specifies the prior distributions and the likelihood, whose contributions are added to the log density.

The complete model is presented below and we will described each block.

```{.stan filename="stan/02_hmm.stan"}
// data
data {
  int<lower=1> T;  // number of observations
  int<lower=1> m;  // number of states
  array[T] real y;  // observations, y coincides with the name in stan_data
}

// parameters
parameters{
    array[m] real mu;                   // means of state dependent distributions
    array[m] real <lower=0> sigma;      // standard deviation of state dependent distributions
    array[m] simplex[m] gamma;          // rows of Gamma, gamma[i] is the i-th row 
    
}

// transformed parameters
transformed parameters{
    matrix[m,m] Gamma;
    row_vector<lower=0, upper=1>[m] delta;


    for (i in 1:m){
        Gamma[i] = gamma[i]';
    }
    delta = rep_row_vector(1, m)/(identity_matrix(m) - Gamma + rep_matrix(1,m,m));
}

// model
model{

    vector[m] log_alpha;

    // Prior of the means
    mu ~ normal(0,5);

    // Prior of the deviation
    sigma ~ normal(0,2); // Restriction on sigma guarantees this is half normal

    // Prior of Gamma
    for (i in 1:m){
        gamma[i] ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1,m));
    }

    // initialize forward log-weights
    for (j in 1:m) {
        log_alpha[j] = log(delta[j]) + normal_lpdf(y[1] | mu[j], sigma[j]);
    }

    // Verosimilitud
    for (t in 2:T){
        vector[m] log_alpha_new;
        for (j in 1:m){
            log_alpha_new[j] = log_sum_exp(log_alpha + log(Gamma[, j])) + normal_lpdf(y[t] | mu[j], sigma[j]);
        }
        log_alpha = log_alpha_new;        
    }
    target += log_sum_exp(log_alpha);
}
```

    delta = rep_row_vector(1, m)/(identity_matrix(m) - Gamma + rep_matrix(1,m,m));

// model
model{

    vector[m] log_alpha;

    // Prior of the means
    mu ~ normal(0,5);

    // Prior of the deviation
    sigma ~ normal(0,2); // Restriction on sigma guarantees this is half normal

    // Prior of Gamma
    for (i in 1:m){
        gamma[i] ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1,m));
    }

    // initialize forward log-weights
    for (j in 1:m) {
        log_alpha[j] = log(delta[j]) + normal_lpdf(y[1] | mu[j], sigma[j]);
    }

    // Verosimilitud
    for (t in 2:T){
        vector[m] log_alpha_new;
        for (j in 1:m){
            log_alpha_new[j] = log_sum_exp(log_alpha + log(Gamma[, j])) + normal_lpdf(y[t] | mu[j], sigma[j]);

We start with the `data` block, where we declare the number of observations $T$, the number of states $m$ and the observations $\mathbf{y}$. *Stan* is statically typed, so every variable must be declared together with its type. Here $T$ and $m$ are integers and $\mathbf{y}$ is an array of $T$ real numbers. The constraint `<lower=1>` states that $T$ and $m$ must be at least one. In the `data` block, constraints act as checks, so *Stan* stops with an error if the data passed to the program do not satisfy them. Note also that the names declared in this block must match exactly the keys of the dictionary passed from *Python*.

```{.stan}
data {
  int<lower=1> T;   // number of observations
  int<lower=1> m;   // number of states
  array[T] real y;  // observations
}
```

The `parameters` block declares the unknown quantities whose posterior distribution we want to explore. Here we declare the means $\mu_j$ and standard deviations $\sigma_j$ of the state-dependent distributions, and the rows $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i$ of the transition probability matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$. Unlike in the `data` block, constraints here define the space explored by the sampler. The constraint `<lower=0>` restricts each $\sigma_j$ to positive values, and the type `simplex[m]` restricts each row of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ to the probability simplex $\Delta^{m-1}$ defined in @sec-priors, so that its entries are non-negative and sum to one. *Stan* enforces these constraints internally by transforming the parameters to an unconstrained space. Note that the initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ is not declared here, since under the stationarity assumption it is a deterministic function of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ and is computed in the next block.

```{.stan}
parameters {
  array[m] real mu;              // means of the state-dependent distributions
  array[m] real<lower=0> sigma;  // standard deviations of the state-dependent distributions
  array[m] simplex[m] gamma;     // rows of Gamma, gamma[i] is the i-th row
}
```
The `transformed parameters` block defines quantities that are computed deterministically from the parameters. They are recomputed at every iteration of the sampler and stored in the output, so their posterior distribution can be summarized in the same way as that of the parameters. Here we compute two such quantities. First, we assemble the transition probability matrix $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ from its rows. Since each `gamma[i]` is a column vector while the rows of a matrix are row vectors, each row is transposed with the operator `'` before being assigned. Second, we compute the stationary distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ using @eq-stationary-solution. Instead of inverting the matrix $\mathbf{I}_m - \boldsymbol{\Gamma} + \mathbf{U}$ explicitly, we use the right division operator `/`, which solves the corresponding linear system and is numerically more stable. The constraint `<lower=0, upper=1>` on `delta` does not restrict the sampler, as it does in the `parameters` block, but acts as a check. If the computed values fall outside this range, which can happen when $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is numerically close to a reducible matrix, *Stan* rejects the proposal and continues sampling.

```{.stan}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[m, m] Gamma;                       // transition probability matrix
  row_vector<lower=0, upper=1>[m] delta;    // stationary distribution

  for (i in 1:m) {
    Gamma[i] = gamma[i]';
  }
  delta = rep_row_vector(1, m) / (identity_matrix(m) - Gamma + rep_matrix(1, m, m));
}
```

The `model` block specifies the two components of the log posterior in @eq-log-posterior, namely the prior distributions of the parameters declared in the `parameters` block and the likelihood. We use the following priors, which correspond to @eq-emission-priors with $\mu_0 = 0$, $s_0 = 5$ and $s_1 = 2$.

- A $\mathcal{N}(0, 5^2)$ prior for each mean $\mu_j$.
- A half-$\mathcal{N}(0, 2^2)$ prior for each standard deviation $\sigma_j$, obtained by combining a normal distribution centered at zero with the constraint `<lower=0>` declared in the `parameters` block.
- A $\text{Dir}(\mathbf{1}_m)$ prior for each row of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$, stored in the array `gamma`.

These priors are weakly informative, since their scales are wide relative to the scale of the data, and they are the same for every state, so the prior is exchangeable in the sense of @sec-exchangeability. No prior is placed on $\boldsymbol{\delta}$, which under the stationarity assumption is computed from $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ in the `transformed parameters` block. 

Once defined the priors on the parameters, the likelihood is evaluated with the forward algorithm. *Stan* actually evaluates the log-likelihood and in order to undertand the code, we write the formula here

Once the priors are specified, the likelihood is evaluated with the forward algorithm. Let $\alpha_t(j)$ denote the joint probability of the observations $y_1, \dots, y_t$ and of being in state $j$ at time $t$. The forward algorithm computes these quantities recursively, and the likelihood is obtained by summing them over the states at the final time $T$ [@zucchini2016]. 

Since the product of many densities quickly underflows to zero, *Stan* works with logarithms, so the recursion is written in terms of $\ell_t(j) = \log \alpha_t(j)$. The forward algorithm, however, requires adding probabilities, and the logarithm of a sum is not the sum of the logarithms. Given the logarithms $x_1, \dots, x_m$ of several probabilities, the logarithm of their sum is

$$
\text{LSE}(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \log \sum_{i=1}^{m} e^{x_i},
$$ {#eq-lse}

which *Stan* implements as `log_sum_exp`. 

For the forward algorithm, we first declare the vector `log_alpha` and initialize it for the first observation

$$
\ell_1(j) = \log \delta_j + \log p_j(y_1), \qquad j = 1, \dots, m,
$$ {#eq-forward-init}

Next, for $t = 2, \dots, T$, we update each $\ell_t(j)$ as

$$
\ell_t(j) = \text{LSE}\big(\ell_{t-1}(1) + \log \gamma_{1j}, \dots, \ell_{t-1}(m) + \log \gamma_{mj}\big) + \log p_j(y_t), \qquad j = 1, \dots, m.
$$ {#eq-forward-step}

Finally, the log-likelihood is obtained by applying the log-sum-exp function in @eq-lse to the values at the last time point,

$$
\log L(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y}) = \text{LSE}\big(\ell_T(1), \dots, \ell_T(m)\big),
$$ {#eq-forward-final}

and it is added to `target`, the variable in which *Stan* accumulates the log posterior density. Together with the contributions of the priors, `target` then holds the value of @eq-log-posterior at the current value of the parameters.

```{.stan}
model{

    vector[m] log_alpha;

    // Prior of the means
    mu ~ normal(0,5);

    // Prior of the deviation
    sigma ~ normal(0,2); // Restriction on sigma guarantees this is half normal

    // Prior of Gamma
    for (i in 1:m){
        gamma[i] ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1,m));
    }

    // initialize forward log-weights
    for (j in 1:m) {
        log_alpha[j] = log(delta[j]) + normal_lpdf(y[1] | mu[j], sigma[j]);
    }

    // Verosimilitud
    for (t in 2:T){
        vector[m] log_alpha_new;
        for (j in 1:m){
            log_alpha_new[j] = log_sum_exp(log_alpha + log(Gamma[, j])) + normal_lpdf(y[t] | mu[j], sigma[j]);
        }
        log_alpha = log_alpha_new;        
    }
    target += log_sum_exp(log_alpha);
}
```

We have a *Stan* model and now we have to fit it.  To fit the model from *Python*, we first load the simulated data and arrange them in a dictionary whose keys match the names declared in the `data` block. Note that the true hidden states stored in the file are not passed to *Stan*, since in a real application they would not be observed. We then compile the program with *CmdStanPy*, which translates it into *C++* and builds an executable. Compilation can take about a minute the first time, but the executable is reused in later runs as long as the `.stan` file does not change.

We then draw samples from the posterior with the `sample` method. We run eight chains in parallel, each starting from a different random initial value, and fix the seed so that the results are reproducible. By default, each chain performs 1000 warmup iterations, which are used to tune the sampler and are discarded, followed by 1000 sampling iterations. The `summary` method reports, for each parameter, the posterior mean and quantiles together with the convergence diagnostics $\hat{R}$ and the effective sample size.

Let's analyze the results from thge summary starting with the convergence diagnostic $\hat{R}$, which compares the variance of the draws between chains with the variance within each chain. Values close to one indicate that all chains explored the same distribution, and @vehtari2021 recommend $\hat{R} < 1.01$, although a looser threshold of $1.05$ is also commonly used.

In our example, only the standard deviations $\sigma_j$ have $\hat{R}$ close to one, while the means $\mu_j$, the transition probabilities in $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ and the stationary distribution $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ show values above 1.6 and require more discussion. 

Since the true standard deviations are equal in both states, swapping the labels leaves them unchanged, whereas the means take different values in each state. The high $\hat{R}$ therefore indicates that different chains settled on different labelings of the states, which is confirmed by the value of $\hat{R}$ close to one for `lp__`, since all chains reach regions of the same posterior density.

Now, let's see the summary statistics of the parameters. The posterior means of $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are closer to zero rather than near their true values of $-2$ and $2$, while their 5th and 95th percentiles are close to $-2$ and $2$. The draws therefore concentrate around both true values, depending on the chain, and the posterior mean falls between them, at a value that no chain actually visits. 

This phenomenon is known as **label switching**. It is a consequence of the posterior symmetry in @eq-posterior-symmetry, whereby every mode has $m!$ copies that differ only in the labeling of the states. Label switching can occur within a chain, when the sampler moves from one copy to another, or between chains, when each chain remains in a single copy but different chains settle on different ones. Our example corresponds to the second case, since the well-separated means make it unlikely for a chain to cross the region of low posterior density between copies. In either case, pooling the draws mixes different labelings, and, as noted by @jasra2005, averages of state-specific quantities become meaningless.

To see why how the sampler moves from one copy to another, we calculate mean summaries of the parameters for each chain. It is observed that that the posterior means of $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ alternate between values close to $-2$ and $2$, the values of the rows of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ alternate between $\begin{bmatrix} 0.80 \ 0.20 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} 0.30 \ 0.70 \end{bmatrix}$ and the values of the stationary distribution alternate between $\begin{bmatrix} 0.60 \ 0.40 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} 0.40 \ 0.60 \end{bmatrix}$. Meanwhile, the mean of `lp__` is nearly the same across chains, which confirms that the chains are exploring equivalent copies of the same mode rather than different modes.

# 3 Label switching {#sec-label-switching}

In @sec-exchangeability we showed that, under an exchangeable prior, the posterior distribution is invariant to permutations of the state labels (@eq-posterior-symmetry). As a consequence, the posterior has $m!$ identical copies, one for each labelling of the states. Label switching occurs when the MCMC draws come from more than one of these copies, so that a given label $j$ does not refer to the same state across draws. Switches can happen within a single chain or between chains.

Label switching does not mean that the sampler has failed. A sampler that explores the full posterior should visit all copies [@jasra2005]. The problem lies in the interpretation of the output. Any summary that depends on the labels, such as the posterior mean of $\mu_1$ or the decoded state probabilities, averages over different states and does not describe any of them. Quantities that are invariant to the labels, such as the log posterior density, remain valid. To make inference about state-specific parameters, we therefore need a way to assign the labels consistently across draws.

In this section we give an introduction to three methods for addresing label switching, properly, *ordering constraints*, *post-hoc relabeling* and *invariant quantities*. Each method has its own advantages and disadvantages so they are discussed as well as . 

## 3.1 Ordering constraints

@jasra2005 and @leosbarajas2018 suggest imposing constraints on the parameters can improve inference on the parameters. A natural choice is to order one parameter of the state-dependent distributions, for example the means, $\mu_1 < \mu_2 < \cdots < \mu_m$. Under this constraint, only one of the $m!$ copies of the posterior remains.

This approach works well when the marginal posteriors of the ordered parameters, within a single copy, do not overlap. When they do overlap, the constraint truncates the posterior and biases the estimates, because the boundary $\mu_j = \mu_{j+1}$ cuts through regions of high posterior density.

Using the example exposed in @sec-stan-implementation, we can impose restrictions on the means $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$. This is achived in *Stan* by replacing the definition of `mu` in the block `parameters`.

```{.stan}
// parameters
parameters{
    ordered[m] mu; // means of state dependent distributions (now is a ordered array)
    
    // Rest of the code    
}
```

We have a *Stan* program with the ordering constraint stored in `stan/02_ex1_normal_order.stan`. We compile it and fit it to the same data with the same settings as before. Unlike the unconstrained fit, all $\hat{R}$ values are now close to one, so we have convergence. The posterior means of $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are $-2.10$ and $1.92$, close to the true values of $-2$ and $2$.

The constraint works well in this example because the marginal posteriors of $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ do not overlap. The 95th percentile of $\mu_1$ is $-1.99$, well below the 5th percentile of $\mu_2$, which is $1.77$. The boundary $\mu_1 = \mu_2$ therefore lies in a region with no posterior mass.

## 3.2 Post-hoc relabelling

Relabelling algorithms are a class of methods for dealing with label switching that rely on Bayesian decision theory [@stephens2000; @jasra2005]. Summarizing the posterior, for example by reporting a point estimate of the state-specific parameters, can be seen as choosing an action $a$ from a set of possible actions $\mathcal{A}$.  This summary, called an action $a$ can be a point estimate of the stet-specific parameters (such as $\mu_j$ or $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$) or the probabilities $P(C_t = j| \mathbf{y})$ of each state at time $t$. Each cpice of action comes weith a loss function $\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{A} \times\boldsymbol{\theta}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ that measures how far $a$ is from the parameters, and the best acttion is the one that minimizes the posterior expected loss [@stephens2000].  

For this, suppose that there is a function $\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{A} \times\boldsymbol{\theta}\rightarrow[0, \infty]$n such that 

$$
L(a,\boldsymbol{\theta})=\underset{\nu \in S_{m}}{\text{min}}{\{L_{0}(a, \nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}))\}}
$$

That is, $L(a,\boldsymbol{\theta})$ measures the loss with respect to the relabelling of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ that is closest to $a$. As a result, $L$ is invariant to permutations of the labels, since $L(a, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = L(a, \nu(\boldsymbol{\theta}))$ for every $\nu \in S_m$.

In practice, we have samples of the parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(2)}, \dots, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(N)}$ from a particular chain, that we assume is stationary. One way to compute the expected posterior loss is by *Monte Carlo*

$$
\mathbb{E}(L(a,\boldsymbol{\theta})) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \min_{\nu_t} \left[ L_0\{a;\, \nu_t(\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)})\} \right]
= \min_{\nu_1, \dots, \nu_N} \left[ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} L_0\{a;\, \nu_t(\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)})\} \right]
$$ {#eq-relabel-risk}

In this notebook we introduced the Bayesian approach to HMMs. We showed that, under exchangeable priors, the posterior is symmetric with respect to the labels of the states, and that this symmetry gives rise to label switching that in practice causes each chain to settle in one of the $m!$ copies or alternate within. 

In our example, label switching produced high values of the $\hat{R}$ convergence diagnostic of the parameters, while the $\hat{R}$ of the log-posterior showed that all chains reached regions of the same posterior density. An ordering constraint on the means removed the symmetry and, since the states were well separated, recovered the true parameters.

The behaviour of the chains is the main lesson for what follows. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo explores the region around its starting point efficiently, but it rarely crosses regions of low posterior density between modes. With label switching this is harmless, since all copies are equivalent and any of them describes the same model. 

When the posterior has genuinely different modes, that is, modes that are not permutations of each other, the same behaviour becomes a serious problem. Each chain may describe a different explanation of the data, and running several chains can reveal this disagreement but cannot tell us how much posterior mass each mode carries. Ordering constraints and relabelling do not help either, because they only remove the symmetry between labels.

In the following notebooks we build a scenario with genuine multimodality, for example by fitting a model with more states than those used to simulate the data, and study how the general-purpose sampler fails on it. 

We then introduce parallel tempering, which runs chains on a sequence of tempered distributions and swaps states between them to move across modes, and implement it with *Pigeons.jl* on the same *Stan* models.
